cards.explanation: The answer is blameless and upright. That's the opening line on Job: "…blameless and upright, fearing God and shunning evil." The writer gives us his character before anything happens to him. I'd love an introduction like that, friends. Mine would be "came out of a closing bakery with a price sticker on him."

The answer is True. Verse 3 says, "Job was the greatest man of all the people of the East." It comes right after the list of his flocks, herds and servants. Friends, that list of animals alone would fill a whole lot of cookie boxes.

The answer is that he offers burnt offerings for them. He sends for his children to purify them, then rises early in the morning to offer burnt offerings for all of them. The text says this was Job's regular practice. Friends, I can barely get up early for a fresh batch.

The answer is that he thinks they may have sinned. The text gives us Job's own thought: "Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts." That's why he offers burnt offerings for all of them. I think that tells us how seriously Job takes his children's hearts.

The answer is False. It wasn't a one-time thing. Verse 5 says, "This was Job’s regular practice." Each time the days of feasting were over, he rose early to offer burnt offerings for his children. That's a man who keeps showing up, friends.

The answer is from roaming through the earth. The full answer Satan gives is, "From roaming through the earth, and walking back and forth in it." The LORD asks where he's come from, and that's what Satan says. Short and plain, friends, no extra details.

The answer is True. The LORD calls Job "My servant" and says, "…there is no one on earth like him…" Then He adds that Job is blameless, upright, fears God and shuns evil. It's the same description the writer gave us in verse 1.

The answer is that Job fears God only because God blesses him. Satan asks, "Does Job fear God for nothing?" Then he points to the hedge around Job and the blessing on the work of his hands. His claim is that Job's fear of God depends on what he gets. Satan is accusing him, friends.

The answer is curse. Satan says, "…he will surely curse You to Your face." That's his bet. He says Job's loyalty will crack once his stuff is struck. The rest of this passage shows what Job actually does, friends.
The answer is True. The LORD says, "Everything he has is in your hands, but you must not lay a hand on the man himself." So Satan gets a limit. He can touch what Job owns, but not Job himself.

The answer is that raiders took them away. The first messenger says the Sabeans swooped down and took the oxen and donkeys away. It happens while the animals are plowing and grazing nearby. That's a rough way to start the news, friends.
The answer is True. Verse 16 says, "While he was still speaking, another messenger came…" Job doesn't get a breath between reports. The news keeps coming, friends.

The answer is that fire fell from heaven and burned them. The second messenger says, "The fire of God fell from heaven. It burned and consumed the sheep and the servants…" This one doesn't come from raiders. The sheep and the servants are both gone, friends.
The answer is camels. The Chaldeans formed three bands, raided the camels and took them away. Job had 3,000 camels (Job 1:3). The third messenger arrives while the second is still speaking, friends.

The answer is wind. The messenger says, "…a mighty wind swept in from the desert and struck the four corners of the house." It collapsed on the young people, and they are dead. This is the heaviest news of the four, friends. I think this one hurts the most.

The answer is that he falls to the ground and worships. Verse 20 says, "He fell to the ground and worshiped…" He's torn his robe and shaved his head, so he's grieving, and he worships anyway. He doesn't cut off the grief or the worship, friends. I think it's one of the most powerful moments in the Bible.

The answer is that he blesses it. Job says, "Blessed be the name of the LORD." It comes right after, "The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away." He has just heard four messengers bring report after report of loss, and that's what he says, friends. It's quiet and it's real.

The answer is False. Job 1:22 says, "In all this, Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing." He has lost his sheep, his camels and his children, and the text still says that, friends. Satan said Job would curse God, and he didn't.
